title: Design a distributed rate limiter
relevance: High — classic standalone HLD prompt (Alex Xu Vol.1 ch.4); also a building-block follow-up inside API, social, payments, and gateway designs (campus + experienced; FAANG and Indian product cos).
company_notes: Very frequent standalone campus/intern HLD and abuse-control follow-up in URL shortener, Twitter, ticket booking, auth; experienced rounds deepen Redis Lua races, Cluster/hash tags, hot keys, fail-open, multi-DC, and rate-limit vs load shedding at Amazon, Google, Meta, Uber, Stripe-like API cos, Atlassian, Flipkart; Alex Xu Vol.1 ch.4 classic and near-universal on public API designs.

phases.goal: Clarify server-side limiter scope, identity keys, reject vs throttle, and NFRs before designing.

must_hit.point: Identify clients via layered keys (user ID / API key when authed, IP for anonymous) and apply the most restrictive of per-user, per-IP, and per-endpoint rules.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names user/API-key vs IP and says layer rules, taking the strictest.

must_hit.point: Enforce configurable quotas and on exceed return HTTP 429 with Limit/Remaining/Reset and Retry-After headers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions 429 plus the standard rate-limit and Retry-After headers.

must_hit.point: NFR: low hot-path overhead aiming under about 5–10 ms added latency, high availability, and slight over/under-count across nodes often acceptable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States latency budget and accepts approximate distributed counts.

must_hit.point: Draw scope: out of analytics warehouse on every deny, strong global consistency across continents, and billing-grade exact metering unless asked.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly parks global strong consistency and billing-grade metering.

probes: Is this a server-side API limiter? Per-user, IP, or API key? Soft throttle or hard reject? Is approximate OK?

hints.1: Start by clarifying identity and whether over/under-count is acceptable.
hints.2: Separate functional (identify, enforce, 429+headers) from NFRs (latency, availability, multi-replica).
hints.3: Layer user+IP+endpoint; aim low added latency; park strong multi-continent consistency and billing-grade metering.

phases.goal: Size Redis check capacity, shard count, and per-key memory for the chosen scale.

must_hit.point: At peak about 1M req/s through the gateway with a huge key space (example 100M users, sparse active set).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses ~1M peak QPS and large distinct-key space like 100M users.

must_hit.point: Budget roughly 50k–100k Lua checks/s per Redis primary, implying about 10–20+ Redis primaries or Redis Cluster for 1M checks/s.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Divides gateway QPS by per-primary check budget to justify many shards/Cluster.

must_hit.point: Token bucket state is about 2 numbers plus TTL per active key; sliding log of timestamps blows memory at this scale.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts compact token-bucket keys with memory-heavy sliding log.

must_hit.point: Counters are ephemeral with TTL/idle expiry; disk DBs are too slow on the request path so an in-memory store is mandatory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects durable disk DB on the hot path in favor of in-memory Redis-like store.

probes: Walk the back-of-envelope: peak QPS, Redis checks per primary, how many shards, and memory per algorithm.

hints.1: Pick a concrete peak QPS with the interviewer before sharding math.
hints.2: Estimate checks/s per Redis primary, then how many primaries for peak gateway QPS.
hints.3: ~1M req/s, ~50k–100k checks/s per primary → ~10–20+ primaries; token bucket ≈ 2 ints + TTL; no disk DB on path.

phases.goal: Define the gateway-internal allow check and the client-visible 429 response contract.

must_hit.point: Internal check shape: isAllowed(clientId, ruleId) returns allowed, remaining, resetAt, and optional retryAfterSec.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes a middleware/RPC allow API returning remaining and reset metadata.

must_hit.point: On deny, clients see HTTP 429 with X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset, and Retry-After.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists 429 and the X-RateLimit-* plus Retry-After headers.

must_hit.point: Optional admin/config CRUD for rules (limit, window, burst, scope = user|ip|key|endpoint|tier) pushed or polled into gateway memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions config CRUD and hot reload into gateway cache without treating limiter as a public product API.

probes: What does the check API return, and what headers does a denied client get?

hints.1: This is gateway-internal middleware, not a public REST rate-limit product.
hints.2: Return allow metadata from the check; map deny to 429 + standard headers.
hints.3: isAllowed → {allowed, remaining, resetAt, retryAfterSec?}; 429 with X-RateLimit-* and Retry-After.

phases.goal: Separate static rules from hot-path Redis bucket/counter keys for one chosen algorithm.

must_hit.point: Rules config fields: ruleId, scope, limit/refill rate, burst capacity, window, endpoints, tier.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists relatively static rule attributes including scope and burst/window.

must_hit.point: Pick one Redis sketch and stick to it: e.g. token bucket hash rl:{client}:{rule} with tokens and last_refill + TTL; fixed window counter; or sliding counter curr/prev windows.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Commits to one algorithm’s key/value layout rather than mixing all.

must_hit.point: Sliding log as a sorted set of timestamps is memory-heavy and usually rejected at this scale.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly discards sliding log for large QPS due to memory.

must_hit.point: With Redis Cluster, use hash tags so multi-key Lua for one client stays on one slot (e.g. {user123}:tokens and {user123}:meta).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions hash tags so EVAL multi-key scripts are single-slot.

probes: What do you store for rules vs for live counters, and how do Cluster hash tags help Lua?

hints.1: Config rules are relatively static; counters/buckets live in Redis on the hot path.
hints.2: Choose one algorithm’s key sketch; mention why sliding log is costly.
hints.3: Token bucket hash with tokens + last_refill + TTL; Cluster hash tags for multi-key Lua.

phases.goal: Place enforcement at the gateway with shared Redis Cluster state and hot-reloaded rules.

must_hit.point: Default path: Client → LB/API Gateway rate-limit middleware → atomic Redis check → allow to API tier or 429.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Draws gateway middleware in front of services with Redis as counter store.

must_hit.point: Redis Cluster is source of truth for counters/buckets, sharded by hash(clientId); sticky sessions are a bad distributed fix.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shards by client id and rejects sticky sessions as the distributed solution.

must_hit.point: Rule config flows disk/DB → workers/push → in-memory cache on gateways so rules change without full redeploy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes Stripe-style push/poll of rules into gateway memory.

must_hit.point: Name alternatives: in-process only under-enforces; dedicated rate-limit microservice adds RTT but richer context; edge PoP is low latency with approximate global.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares local-only, dedicated service, and edge placement tradeoffs.

probes: Where do you place the limiter, and why not only local counters on each app server?

hints.1: Prefer API gateway/middleware so you drop early under one policy.
hints.2: Shared Redis Cluster keyed by client; rules cached on gateways.
hints.3: Gateway middleware + Lua to Redis Cluster sharded by clientId; call out in-process under-enforcement and optional dedicated/edge designs.

phases.goal: Defend algorithm choice, atomic Redis updates, failure mode, and multi-region accuracy.

must_hit.point: Default to token bucket for controlled bursts and good DX; fixed window is a fine start but has a 2× boundary burst; sliding counter for near-sliding accuracy with O(1) memory; leaky/blocking when smoothing outbound to a fragile dependency.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks token bucket as default and can explain fixed-window 2× and when sliding/leaky fit.

must_hit.point: HMGET then HSET/MULTI still races across gateways; entire refill+consume must run in one Lua EVAL/EVALSHA.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects read-then-MULTI and insists on a single atomic Lua script.

must_hit.point: Fail-open for availability (e.g. social/blog under Redis blip, Stripe request limiter) vs fail-closed for payments/LLM cost/security quotas; pair with load shedders for fleet emergencies.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Chooses fail-open vs fail-closed by risk and distinguishes load shedding.

must_hit.point: Exact global multi-DC counts cost RTT/complexity; pragmatic design is per-region or edge limits with slight over-allow.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Accepts per-region approximate caps instead of exact global counters.

probes: Why token bucket over fixed window? What breaks if two gateways check Redis without Lua? Fail-open or fail-closed when Redis is down?

hints.1: Interviewers will poke algorithm boundary behavior and Redis races.
hints.2: Separate algorithm DX, atomicity, and availability-vs-quota failure mode.
hints.3: Token bucket default; Lua for refill+consume; fail-open vs fail-closed by risk; per-region not exact global.

phases.goal: Scale past Redis QPS and hot keys, and operate safely with kill switches and dark-launch.

must_hit.point: Usual ceiling is Redis CPU/QPS → shard by client id, Redis Cluster, and connection pools on gateways.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names Redis throughput as the bottleneck and sharding/pooling as the fix.

must_hit.point: Hot key (one abuser/scraper IP) saturates a shard → local deny cache, stricter IP rules, challenge/ban, or isolate heavy tenants.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Has a concrete hot-key mitigation beyond more generic shards.

must_hit.point: Config fan-out via push plus feature-flag/kill switch to disable enforcement if a bad rule ships; dark-launch before enforce.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions kill switch and dark-launch like Stripe before full enforcement.

must_hit.point: Observe 429s by rule, Redis latency/errors, and fail-open events; co-locate Redis in-region and avoid sticky-session “solutions” for gateway CPU/RTT.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists observability signals and in-region Redis co-location.

probes: What saturates first at high QPS, and how do you handle one mega-client hammering a single shard?

hints.1: Think about Redis as the shared bottleneck, not just gateway CPU.
hints.2: Cover sharding, hot keys, and operational kill switches.
hints.3: Shard/Cluster + pools; hot-key local deny/ban; push rules with kill switch and dark-launch.

tradeoffs.topic: Token bucket vs fixed window vs sliding counter vs leaky bucket
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Token bucket is the usual default (controlled burst b, sustained refill r, good mobile/batch DX). Fixed window is simple but allows ~2× at the boundary. Sliding counter (Cloudflare) gives near-sliding accuracy with O(1) memory. Leaky/blocking (e.g. Uber lib) smooths outbound to fragile dependencies with little/no burst.

tradeoffs.topic: Fail-open vs fail-closed on Redis failure
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Fail-open preserves availability for social/blog-style APIs (Stripe request limiter) with alerts; fail-closed protects payments, LLM cost, and security quotas. Keep separate load shedders for fleet-health emergencies rather than conflating them with per-identity quotas.

tradeoffs.topic: Exact global multi-DC counts vs per-region / edge limits
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Exact global counters add high RTT and complexity; practical designs use per-region or edge limits and accept slight over-allow, optionally with careful local “already denied” caches under attack.

tradeoffs.topic: Gateway middleware vs dedicated rate-limit service vs in-process only
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Gateway middleware drops early under one policy. In-process counters under-enforce by about replica count. A dedicated service can use richer app context but adds an RTT. Edge PoPs cut latency with approximate global behavior.

gotchas.trap: Putting a counter only on each app server
gotchas.correction: Local counters under-enforce by about N replicas; use a shared Redis (or equivalent) for distributed quotas.

gotchas.trap: Fixed window feels correct on the whiteboard
gotchas.correction: Probe the double-limit / 2× burst at the window edge; fix with sliding counter/log or token bucket.

gotchas.trap: Treating token bucket as unlimited burst
gotchas.correction: Burst capacity b caps the spike; refill rate caps the long-term average.

gotchas.trap: Using MULTI after a separate non-atomic read for check-and-consume
gotchas.correction: Two gateways can both see the same remaining tokens; put refill+consume in one Lua EVAL (or a single INCR for simple windows).

gotchas.trap: Staying silent when Redis is down
gotchas.correction: Explicitly choose and justify fail-open vs fail-closed for the product’s risk.

gotchas.trap: Conflating rate limiting with load shedding
gotchas.correction: Rate limit is per-identity quota; load shedding drops low-priority traffic for fleet health (Stripe’s split).

gotchas.trap: IP-only limits as the sole identity
gotchas.correction: NAT/CGNAT and office Wi-Fi cause false positives; prefer authenticated identity when available and layer keys.
Exact global counts are expensive; per-region or edge with slight over-allow is the pragmatic answer.
